must_ask.say: Is the headache worse in the morning?
How many weeks has the headache lasted?

history.answer: I had a seizure yesterday out of nowhere, and my head has been aching terribly every morning for the past month.
My husband said I suddenly went stiff, fell onto the couch, and began violently shaking all over with my eyes rolled upward.
He told me the whole shaking lasted about two to three minutes, and it only happened that one time without repeating.
I don't remember any warning signs like strange smells, a rising stomach sensation, or dizziness; I just blacked out completely.
My husband didn't see one specific limb twitching first, but he noticed my head and eyes seemed turned toward the left when it started.
I didn't bite my tongue or cheeks, but my husband said I lost bladder control and wet my pants.
I was groggy, confused, and had trouble recognizing what happened for about thirty minutes after waking up, and all my muscles felt deeply sore.
Thankfully I collapsed onto the living room sofa, so I didn't strike my head or hurt my shoulders.
No, this was the very first seizure I have ever had. I have never had blackouts, staring spells, or morning jerks.
I have not had any fever, chills, neck stiffness, or continuous loss of consciousness.
It started a month ago as a dull ache all over my head, but it has steadily gotten more intense and throbbing, especially right when I wake up in the morning.
The headache gets noticeably worse when I bend over to tie my shoes, cough, or strain on the toilet.
I have had queasiness and mild nausea almost every morning along with the headache, though I haven't thrown up.
Now that I think about it, my left hand has felt a bit clumsy and weak when holding plates over the past couple of weeks.
My husband mentioned that I have seemed more irritable, forgetful, and slower to respond to questions over the past month.
I wasn't sleep-deprived, sick, stressed, or around flashing lights before this happened.
I do not drink alcohol at all, and I have never taken any illicit drugs or sedatives.
I don't have diabetes, I don't take insulin or blood sugar pills, and my eating has been regular without vomiting or diarrhea.
I have never had any head injuries, concussions, stroke, meningitis, or brain surgery.
history.topic: Past head trauma and neurological illness

history.answer: I hold a driver's license and usually drive for errands, but my husband drove me here today and I will not drive until this is resolved.
My husband was terrified seeing me convulse, and with these worsening morning headaches, I am terrified that I might have a brain tumor.
I want to get a brain MRI done right away and be evaluated by a brain specialist to find out what is wrong.
I have no chronic medical conditions, no high blood pressure, and no heart disease.
I have never undergone any surgical procedures or had any hospital stays.
I do not take any prescribed medications. I only tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen for the headache, but it barely helped.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I am a homemaker and I live at home with my husband.
Nobody in my family has ever had seizures, epilepsy, brain tumors, or neurological conditions.
I went through natural menopause about seven years ago and have not had any bleeding since.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and fingerstick blood glucose 104 mg/dL.
Alert, fully oriented to person, place, and time; speech is fluent, though processing speed appears mildly delayed.
Pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; fundoscopy shows mild bilateral optic disc swelling (papilledema), and there is subtle flattening of the left nasolabial fold.
Normal muscle bulk throughout; motor strength is 4/5 in the left upper extremity with a mild pronator drift, and 5/5 in the right upper extremity and both lower extremities.
Hyperreflexia (3+) at the left biceps and patellar tendons compared to normal (2+) on the right; left Babinski sign is extensor (upgoing toe), right is flexor.
Intact sensation to light touch, pinprick, and vibration symmetrically across all four extremities.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are mildly clumsy on the left; gait is steady without gross ataxia.
Supple neck with full passive flexion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Oral cavity clear; no lateral tongue lacerations, bite wounds, bleeding, or mucosal injury.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
No scalp hematoma, laceration, contusion, or signs of acute bodily trauma.
